claims.text: The starting FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating has BCC phase segregated along grain boundaries.
A controlled thermo-mechanical or cooling treatment can redistribute the BCC phase uniformly within the FCC matrix.
The redistributed BCC phase will form nanoscale precipitates.
A nanoscale BCC dispersion in an FCC matrix produces coherent FCC/BCC interfaces.
The dispersed BCC phase is harder than the ductile FCC matrix.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces impede or pin dislocations.
Dislocation pinning at coherent FCC/BCC interfaces increases local back stress.
The interfaces force dislocations to bypass the BCC obstacles through less efficient mechanisms such as climb.
The proposed obstruction of dislocation motion slows the overall creep strain rate.
A uniformly dispersed nanoscale BCC phase will reduce steady-state creep rate relative to a grain-boundary-segregated BCC baseline.
A uniformly dispersed nanoscale BCC phase will increase creep life relative to a grain-boundary-segregated BCC baseline.
Grain-boundary segregation of BCC phase leads to higher dislocation mobility.
Grain-boundary segregation of BCC phase causes faster creep-strain accumulation.
The proposed mechanism operates at temperatures where dislocation creep dominates.
At very high temperatures where diffusion creep dominates, the benefit of the dispersed BCC phase may diminish.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction is not yet quantified.
The optimal BCC precipitate size and volume fraction are not yet quantified.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing uniformly dispersed and grain-boundary-segregated coatings under identical creep stress and temperature.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-rate decrease or creep-life increase in the uniformly dispersed coating would falsify the hypothesis.
